utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You've told us that you went to both places but you can't remember which place you went to first. Can you recall how you were dressed when you went to either of those two places, the TO or the Buducnost factory, any features of your dress?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I was wearing a tracksuit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other features of your apparel that you can remember, the clothes you had to wear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I can't remember now. Maybe I had a coat on, because it was April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, please, of your visit to the TO, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes. When I heard the announcement that we should all report there, when I left my yard, I ran into a few of my neighbours. So we set out in the direction of the Territorial Defence together. As we approached it, the number of people grew so that when I arrived there, there were some 20 people waiting in a queue in front of me. So I stood in the queue myself. And we had to say when -- our date of birth, our first and last name, and we were not given any specific assignments but simply told to return to our homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnic background of the 20 or so people that were gathered there at the TO with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: When I think of it now, they were all Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Think back now and the clothing that they were wearing. Was there anything about the clothing that they had on that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: All of us who came to report, we were all wearing civilian clothes, civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: May I seek the assistance of the usher, please. I'd like to show Exhibit P14, and in particular -- 14A, I should say, and in particular, photograph number 50. This is the only one that I want to refer to at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It is a set of photographs, quite large photographs. It should be P14A, because that's the one without any headings. MR. DI FAZIO: And perhaps it could be placed on the ELMO so that the witness can just demonstrate where the people were gathered.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: This is -- MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just tell us what building that is, first of all.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: This is the building of the Territorial Defence in my town of Bosanski Samac. This is the main entrance, and this is the room where I went in and stood in the queue waiting to report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Witness, I'd like you to do just exactly the same again, except this time use the metal pointer and point to the photograph on the device just on your right, because then we'll all be able to see it on our TV screens, okay? Just turn around. MR. DI FAZIO: And with the assistance of the usher, he can gently direct the witness to the photograph. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what's that door that you're pointing to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: This is the building of the Territorial Defence in my town. This is the main entrance. This is the first room to the left when you come in where there was a desk with three people sitting behind it making a list of us who were queueing up to give them our details, our names and dates of birth. In front of this building stood an armed soldier with a rifle on his shoulder, and he was wearing a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: I think I've finished with the photograph, Mr. Usher. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Mr. di Fazio, this sort of evidence seems, to my mind, to be repetitive evidence which has never been objected to by the Defence counsel. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: So I'm wondering, is there a need to go through with these sort of details. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, no. If the Chamber is not going to be assisted by that, then I won't take it through in this sort of detail. Alternatively, is Your Honour suggesting I should be leading the witness and getting through it faster? I'm not quite certain -- sure of the position Your Honour is taking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think the point being made is that we've seen this photograph of the territorial building so many times now, so that it may not be necessary for the witness to actually view the photograph and refer to it. I don't think there is any dispute that that is the building of the Territorial Defence. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Okay. I understand that point, and I won't take the witness through it chapter and verse in the manner that I've been doing up until now. And I'm grateful to the Chamber for that. It will assist me to get through this faster. Of course, this evidence that this witness is now giving is from a different perspective, that of a person who was not a prisoner, and from that point of view, of course, it's quite important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the way to the Territorial Defence, was it safe to walk the streets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to take any precautions to ensure that there was some safety at least? Anything you could do to make it safer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes. We crept along next to walls or crossing yards if it was possible. There was constant shooting. We didn't know where the shots were coming from, but we had the feeling that -- well, the armed people we met in the streets yelled, "Snipers. Snipers. There are snipers on the buildings." So sometimes we had to duck, and we had to bend over as we were walking, to run across the street, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you tell us about your visit to the Budcnost factory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I was informed in the same manner that all citizens were to report there, and I again decided to call my neighbours, or maybe they called me, I don't remember, but two or three of us set out together toward the Budcnost furniture factory. As we approached it, the group grew. When we arrived in the yard of the Budcnost building, there were about 150 of my fellow citizens there already. We were all unarmed, and we were civilians wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you comment on the ethnic background of the civilians who were assembled there, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Well, now that I think about it, they were all Croats or Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: We waited to hear what Jovo Lukic would tell us. He had been appointed commander of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you -- did you know that he'd been appointed commander of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: That's how he introduced himself. And behind his back there were a few stairs, and then he climbed up to the top and then he introduced himself as such.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What else did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: He said we were to be quiet, that Serbian forces had entered our town, that there was no reason to worry, that we should simply obey orders, and that nothing bad would happen to any of us, that we should all join together to preserve the town from attacks by extremists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the meeting interrupted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes, it was interrupted, because a truck arrived from the direction of the city centre, with three or four armed soldiers on it, and they asked for Igor Rukavina from our group, accusing him of being a sniper operator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes. He was in our group. He was reluctant to report. It seemed to me that a long time had passed, but several of us saw him among us. But we all waited for him to declare himself, and when he finally mustered the courage, he was brutally pushed in the truck. And we were told from the truck to disperse, and if someone had any questions, he should ask General Adzic, who was the commander of the Yugoslav army at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Following the meeting, did you go home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes. The new commander of the TO had the same opinion. He said, "We'll disperse now. Go to your homes." And we set out in groups toward the centre, and I went to my house. There was shooting again. Allegedly it was snipers. So we stayed close to fences and crept along. That's how my fellow citizens and I moved along, and in this manner, I reached my house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Sorry. Perhaps we may stop here. The Trial Chamber was informed that there are some matters the Defence counsel would like to raise. And perhaps you can release the witness and let him leave the courtroom. The proceedings will continuing tomorrow - this is for the witness - and he will be informed at what time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Actually, there are two things which I wanted to raise with the -- and I informed the Registry and the Senior Legal Officer about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, the problem which my client faced today, and this is, like, at least the third or the fourth time I have informed the Registry about it. This place where he is kept during the time when he's resting, there is a problem with the heating, and it is very cold down there. And the guards have been helping, trying to fix that, but to no avail. And this creates a lot of problems for my client, because out of staying in a cold room, he is experiencing some problems with his health. That is number one. And I understand this has to be clarified somehow with the Registry, and I informed the Registry Already for -- this is the third time now, and then I needed to raise it right now, here with the Trial Chamber. Of course, this problem comes out only when it is very cold --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because we are moving into winter now. It's been fairly cold the past few days, and even today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Exactly. And the second matter, Your Honours, is that we have raised these questions at least twice right now in these proceedings about the direct versus indirect testimony against my client. Because my client, since he is not feeling well, he would like to rest tomorrow afternoon and not to come into the Court, and I am -- we requested already, as you know, Your Honours, that we have some guidance from this Trial Chamber what is considered direct or indirect evidence against our client. And that is what I would like to clarify before the Trial Chamber decides whether we can work without my client, or rather, that we have simple guidelines so my client knows, when he waives his right, that he exactly knows what might be the -- what is his or our, Defence's, position. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. On the first point, of course the Trial Chamber will follow up the matter with the relevant office. We accept that you did inform the Registry, and of course it's your duty as Defence counsel to deal with the immediate problems of your client. And we do hope that either they will move him to a room where the heating system is working if they can't repair the heating system where he normally rests, but at least to make sure that he's not exposed to the cold, because obviously it will aggravate his poor health.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: On the second question of whether the witness is direct or indirect, we really haven't delved into that and we haven't got that classification of witnesses yet. I know we alluded to it, but we haven't got that classification yet, for the simple reason that the summaries that we have, as we have observed as the witnesses come and give evidence, quite often the evidence goes beyond what appears to be in the summary, so it is difficult for anybody really to tell what the witness will be able to say in the witness box.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours, completely, and that is why I raised this question with the Prosecutor, because the Prosecutor might tell us that. And if the Prosecutor says this is not direct evidence, then we will have to have some kind of assurance in that respect that this is not direct evidence against our client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps that is a matter that can -- I think it was dealt with by the Prosecution, but I don't think sufficiently. And what the Trial Chamber has observed, like I said, the summaries don't appear to be, you know, followed in most of the cases. There's more evidence beyond what the summaries provide. And perhaps that can be looked into to try and see how we can assist the Defence counsel, and Mr. Simic himself, when giving instructions to his counsel as to whether or not he feels he can rest during a particular proceeding during the time that any particular witness is giving evidence. Of course, the ideal situation is to have Mr. Milan Simic in the courtroom so that he can observe the witnesses for himself, and that would normally jog his memory here and there perhaps, and then he would be able to give instructions. We have been informed by the administration that they're looking into the matter of providing the facilities we thought they would be able to provide at the Detention Unit. It will not be possible before the end of the proceedings this year, because of so many reasons which I wouldn't go into, and the fact that some trials are beginning perhaps at the beginning of December. So it may not be possible. They are saying that it may be possible in January, when we start. So that even if he's resting in the Detention Unit, he may be able to follow, if he's in a position to follow the proceedings, and that would be the ideal situation. But as to whether or not the witnesses are direct or indirect, that is a matter which I think we have to go into, we would ask the Prosecution to go into very, very carefully, so that we avoid undermining the basic rights of Mr. Milan Simic when he -- as to when he should -- if he's not feeling well, when he can rest in the Detention Unit, rest assured that he is not missing the opportunity of giving you instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think, besides that, I don't think there is anything we can say right now. If he's not feeling well and he feels like resting tomorrow afternoon, I think that is a matter between you and him. Because I cannot say whether the witness -- this witness or the next one will be direct or indirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I hope you understand that neither my client nor I are willing to stall these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We are really trying to expedite it as much as possible. That is why I raise this question. Otherwise we could just stand up and say that he doesn't feel well. That is why I'm trying to be cooperative in this respect, and that is why I need the guidelines from the Trial Chamber, in order that my client knows exactly what kind of rights he's waiving at a certain moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: At any time. Yes. Yes. Yes. The Trial Chamber accepts what you're saying and your assurance that you are also interested, as is your client, in expediting these proceedings. So I'll ask the Prosecution. I may not ask for direct answers right now, but see what can be done in view of these problems. There's nothing we can do about the witness on the stand right now, because we just have to continue tomorrow. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. If Your Honours please, I understand my learned friend's dilemma, and I sympathise, and the Prosecution will do whatever we can to assist. The question of guidelines, however, is troubling, I think, and this particular witness provides a salutary example. In the course of proofing him, I've ascertained that he mentions Mr. Milan Simic's name briefly in respect of a particular episode that occurred very shortly after the takeover that is not mentioned in his statement. I'm going to inform Mr. Zecevic of that shortly, after we break. In addition, during the afternoon break, having seen some of the documents that were produced, I think, to witnesses while I wasn't here, we ran those documents past the witness and suddenly all this new information is provided, and that illustrates the sort of problem that arises. And I mentioned before that many of these witnesses have given statements back in the mid-1990s, and we proof them just before they come into Court, and the best that you can do is hopefully get to Defence counsel before they're actually in the box. Another example, to be contrasted, is that of Mr. Todorovic. I've been proofing him and I'm getting my notes together, and as soon as that exercise is complete, I'll be able to provide those notes to counsel well in advance. Not all of the notes but disclosure of the new features of evidence to Defence counsel in advance. There won't be a problem there. The problem arises with witnesses just like this one, who arrive shortly before trial, are proofed right up to the point where they walk into court, and because of that, it's very hard to adhere to any sort of guideline and the matter has to be approached, I suggest, on an ad hoc basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It will be witness by witness. MR. DI FAZIO: Witness by witness. And that's really the only effective, practical way of dealing with this matter. Bearing that in mind, of course, the Prosecution will do whatever it can to ensure that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: -- Mr. Simic is told through his counsel which witnesses will be speaking about him directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: As for this witness, Mr. di Fazio, looking at the timetable will you be finished with him by tomorrow 11.00 or 1.00? So that if he's going to be away tomorrow afternoon, then cross-examination is going to start and then he'll be away during cross-examination possibly. MR. DI FAZIO: As -- doing my best, if Your Honours please, my prediction is that I'd be finished with him either very late tomorrow morning or early tomorrow afternoon, I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zecevic, you've heard what Mr. di Fazio has said about the impossible task of being able to ascertain what the witness will say. And this is compounded by the situation, by the fact that most of the Prosecution witnesses do not live in The Hague, I mean, in this country. So there is no opportunity for counsel to see them beforehand, like even a day before, to be able to inform you. So we will just have to do it the best we way we can, and the Prosecution will undertake to inform you as to the particular references regarding your client so that you can get instructions on that and be able to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If you allow me Your Honours, just very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand the situation very clearly. That is why I insisted that we have guidelines from this Honourable Trial Chamber in order that we can decide whether this is direct or indirect evidence. I mean, what this Trial Chamber assumes as a direct or indirect evidence, that is what we would like to know. And then we can only decide whether this is appropriate for us that Mr. Milan Simic waives his right or not. That is the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That is an impossible task for the Trial Chamber, because by the time Mr. di Fazio finishes proofing any his witnesses, there may be just sufficient time to inform you of the details. Perhaps then maybe he may be able to inform the Chamber that actually there is evidence touching on Mr. Milan Simic. But for the Trial Chamber to make -- to make a cutout list that these witnesses are direct, these are indirect, no, because we don't have that concept, at least in the Tribunal. So that makes it difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. I understand very well, Your Honours. But this is the issue that we have raised --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- in this trial before, and that is why I was referring to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. At first it appeared simple, that where a witness is not mentioning Mr. Milan Simic, then one may say that is not -- the evidence does not directly involve Mr. Milan Simic. But you can see the overlap in the evidence of the various Prosecution witnesses. And even though the name may not be mentioned, some of the evidence may be -- may be attributed to the fact that your client was involved, and that is where the problem is. Yes. And then also very much depends on how the questions are put to a witness. And the other problem is a witness may walk in here and look at the defendants and then remember. You see? So it isn't a matter which the Trial Chamber can really decide before the evidence is even heard. It's difficult. So all I can say is we'll leave it to the Prosecution. Once they proof their witnesses, then they discuss with you, and then you discuss with your client. The decision should be yours, between you and your client. It is important that that is done that way, because some of the witnesses who come here, you may know them, your client may know them. We don't know the witnesses. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know them as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Some of them. Maybe your client knows them, yes. So normally you find that some information which the Prosecution or the Defence counsel or indeed the accused may know is not known by the Trial Chamber. So that directed version, no. I don't think we can make that at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We'll rise and continue at -- I'm sorry. Mr. Lukic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. I will take up just one more minute of your time, but I mean to refer directly to the first point that my colleague Mr. Zecevic mentioned. I didn't want to burden the Trial Chamber with the problem of my defendant, which began right at the beginning when we started to have morning and afternoon sessions. I'm talking about the two-and-a-half-hour break. He has considerable problems which could be resolved quite simply. What my colleague Zecevic had said about the cold that we all felt when we went there during the break. My client is 65 years old, and up until recently, he was the eldest accused at the Detention Unit. He has considerable health problems, and there is medical documentation about the treatment he had while he was on temporary release. There are two alternatives. Either he be permitted during that two-and-a-half-hour break to be in the rooms right next to the Trial Chamber - he would be able to be quite comfortable there - and also he would request a slightly softer, more comfortable chair. I really didn't have the intention of bringing this before the Chamber, but since my learned colleague Mr. Zecevic has already mentioned a problem of this kind, we're all very concerned about the health of our clients and -- so that they are able to follow the proceedings in the most comfortable and the best possible way. This is all I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I just want it to be clear. Does your client wait in the same room that Mr. Milan Simic waits in during the lunch break? Is it the same room?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are all in similar rooms which are next to one another downstairs. I don't know which room Mr. Simic is in, but I was in one of those rooms. There are plastic chairs there that are attached to the floor and you cannot move them, and they're very uncomfortable to sit in, especially for older people. And unfortunately, I have to treat him in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. It is important that you bring the health concerns of your clients to the attention of the Trial Chamber, yes, because of the obvious reasons that, you know, we're supposed to make sure as much as possible the accused persons are looked after during the proceedings and in that way they're able to follow the proceedings properly. The Trial Chamber will deal with these matters by raising them with the relevant offices, and we are very hopeful that something will be done. Either the rooms will be improved or portable heaters maybe can be provided, but we'll leave that to the people concerned. But we'll make emphasis on that. We're not prepared to kill the accused slowly, if I dare say that. We're really interested in their health. We will adjourn and continue our proceedings tomorrow morning at 21 0930 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 21 day of November, 2001, at 9.30 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.14 p.m.,
